conclusion: Two copies of the 677T version. Compared with people carrying the common version, the enzyme is less heat-stable and less active, and blood homocysteine runs measurably higher. A raised homocysteine level is a lab finding, not a disease; what it means for heart or pregnancy outcomes is debated and is not stated here.

One copy of each variant, on opposite chromosomes, so neither chromosome carries the common version. In the study that described it this combination looked like having two 677T copies: lower enzyme activity, higher homocysteine and lower blood folate.

Two copies of the 1298C version. Enzyme activity is somewhat lower than with the common version, but blood homocysteine and folate were not different. No noticeable difference is expected from this alone.
One copy of the 677T version. The enzyme is somewhat less active; the raised homocysteine reported for this variant was for two copies. No noticeable difference is known for one copy.
One copy of the 1298C version. No difference in homocysteine or folate was found. No noticeable difference is expected.
The most common version on both chromosomes at these two positions. Rarer MTHFR variants are not looked at here.

Both variants on one chromosome and the common version on the other. One chromosome still carries the common version, so the expectation is that of carrying a single 677T copy rather than the combination above. The papers read here do not describe this arrangement; it is stated so that it is not mistaken for the two-chromosome case.
